prompt: `io` declares `type ReadWriter interface { Reader; Writer }`, each on its own line. What does that declaration mean?
hint: What does an interface consist of?

choices.text: A `ReadWriter` holds a `Reader` value and a `Writer` value, like two struct fields
choices.why: An interface holds one value, of one dynamic type. Its declaration lists methods, not fields.

choices.text: Its method list is `Read` and `Write`, the methods of both
choices.why: Right. Embedding adds the embedded interface's methods to the list, and that is all it does.

choices.text: A type must declare that it extends `Reader` and `Writer`
choices.why: Nothing is declared anywhere; a type satisfies `ReadWriter` by having both methods, as lesson 27 said.

choices.text: Either a `Read` or a `Write` method is enough
choices.why: Either one is not enough: `*strings.Reader` has `Read` and was refused for missing `Write`.

prompt: Which of these types satisfies `io.ReadWriteCloser`?
hint: It asks for `Read`, `Write` and `Close`.

choices.text: `*bytes.Buffer`
choices.why: It reads and writes, and the compiler refused it for `missing method Close`.

choices.text: `*strings.Reader`
choices.why: It only reads a string; it was refused even as an `io.ReadWriter`.

choices.text: `*os.File`
choices.why: Right. `var rwc io.ReadWriteCloser = os.Stdout` compiled, and `%T` printed `*os.File`.

choices.text: `*bufio.Writer`
choices.why: It writes and flushes, but it has no `Read` and no `Close` method.

prompt: `var r io.Reader = &buf` holds a `*bytes.Buffer`, which has `Write`. Why is `var rw io.ReadWriter = r` refused?
hint: What does the compiler know about `r`?

choices.text: One interface can never be assigned to another
choices.why: `var r io.Reader = rw` compiled in the same section: bigger to smaller is fine.

choices.text: The compiler judges `r` by its type, and `io.Reader` promises only `Read`
choices.why: Right. What `r` holds is only known at run time, which is where an assertion asks.

choices.text: It needs a conversion, `io.ReadWriter(r)`, to compile
choices.why: A conversion is checked against the same lists and is refused too, with `missing method Write`.

choices.text: A `*bytes.Buffer` loses its `Write` method once stored as an `io.Reader`
choices.why: Nothing is lost: `%T` still prints `*bytes.Buffer`, and section 03 gets `Write` back by asking.

prompt: An interface listed inside another interface adds its ___ to the list, and that is all embedding does.
hint: `Read`, `Write` and `Close` are three of them.

prompt: `io.ReadCloser` and `io.WriteCloser` both include `Close() error`. What happens with `type RWC interface { io.ReadCloser; io.WriteCloser }`?
hint: A method set is a set.

choices.text: The compiler refuses it: `duplicate method Close`
choices.why: That message exists for a module whose `go` line is older than 1.14; on go1.27.1 it compiled.

choices.text: It has two `Close` methods, and a call must say which one
choices.why: A method set has no way to hold two methods of one name; the two are the same method.

choices.text: It has one `Close`, since an identical method counts once
choices.why: Right. `var f ReadWriteCloser = os.Stdout` compiled and ran.

choices.text: The later `Close` hides the earlier one, like a shallower struct field
choices.why: Depth decides between struct fields in lesson 16; here there is nothing to decide, both are `Close() error`.

prompt: `FlushWriter` embeds `io.Writer` and adds `Flush() error`. Which of these can be passed where a `FlushWriter` is asked for? Choose all that apply.
hint: It needs both methods, and nothing declared.

choices.text: A `*bufio.Writer`
choices.why: Yes: `greet(out, "Ana")` compiled and printed `Hello, Ana`.

choices.text: `os.Stdout`
choices.why: Refused: `*os.File does not implement FlushWriter (missing method Flush)`.

choices.text: A type of your own with `Write` and `Flush` methods of the right signatures
choices.why: Yes. Satisfying an interface takes only the methods, whoever wrote the type.

choices.text: A `*bytes.Buffer`
choices.why: It writes, but `bytes.Buffer` has no `Flush`; nothing it holds is waiting to be passed on.

prompt: `doc["name"]` holds the string `"Ana"`. What does `n, ok := doc["name"].(float64)` give?
hint: This is the two-result form.

choices.text: A panic: the value is a string, not a `float64`
choices.why: That is the single-result form. With `ok` there to take the answer, nothing panics.

choices.text: `n` is 0 and `ok` is false
choices.why: Right. The run printed `name   0 false`: the zero value of `float64` and a no.

choices.text: `n` is the string converted to a number, 0 here, and `ok` is true
choices.why: An assertion converts nothing. It checks the dynamic type and answers whether it matched.

choices.text: Nothing: the compiler refuses it, as the map holds a string there
choices.why: The compiler cannot see what a `map[string]any` holds; it accepts every assertion on one.

prompt: The JSON had no `email` key. What does `email := doc["email"].(string)` do?
hint: What does a map give for a key it does not have, and what type is that?

choices.text: `email` is `""`, the zero value of a string
choices.why: Only the two-result form hands back a zero value; this one has nowhere to say no.

choices.text: The compiler refuses to assert on a missing key
choices.why: Which keys exist is only known when the JSON arrives; the line compiled.

choices.text: It panics: the map gave an empty interface, and it holds no string
choices.why: Right: `interface conversion: interface {} is nil, not string`.

choices.text: `email` is nil, since the key is missing
choices.why: `email` would be a `string`, and a string cannot be nil; the program stops before it exists.

prompt: Match each line to what it does when the program is built and run.
hint: Two of them never get to run.

pairs.left: `s, ok := x.(string)` with `x` an `any` holding an `int`

pairs.right: Refused as an impossible type assertion

right_distractors: Converts the value to a string

prompt: `report(w io.Writer, ...)` contains `if f, ok := w.(FlushWriter); ok`. What does that line ask?
hint: `FlushWriter` is an interface, not a concrete type.

choices.text: Whether `w` was declared as a `FlushWriter`
choices.why: `w` was declared `io.Writer`, and that never changes; the question is about the value inside.

choices.text: Whether the value inside `w` also has `Flush() error`
choices.why: Right. Asserting to an interface asks for its methods, whatever the concrete type turns out to be.

choices.text: Whether `w` is a `*bufio.Writer`, the one type with `Flush`
choices.why: Any type with both methods passes, including one you write; the assertion never names `bufio`.

choices.text: Whether `w` is nil
choices.why: That is `w == nil`. An assertion asks about the type inside, and answers false for nil too.

prompt: `io.Copy(os.Stdout, &buf)` copies from a `*bytes.Buffer`. Going by the lines of `copyBuffer` printed in section 03, what does it do first?
hint: Which interface does a `*bytes.Buffer` have a method of?

choices.text: It reads 32 KB at a time and writes each piece
choices.why: That is the loop for readers that answered no; the buffer answers yes before it.

choices.text: It hands the whole job to the buffer's `WriteTo` method
choices.why: Right. `src.(WriterTo)` is the first assertion, and `*bytes.Buffer` has `WriteTo`.

choices.text: It asks the writer for `ReadFrom` before anything else
choices.why: The writer is asked second; the reader's `WriteTo` is checked first.

choices.text: It panics unless the reader has a `WriteTo` method
choices.why: Both assertions use `ok`, so a reader without `WriteTo` is simply copied the slow way.

prompt: A function receives `r io.Reader` and should close it when the value can be closed, and leave it alone otherwise. Which line does that?
hint: Some readers have `Close`, some do not, and `io.Reader` promises only `Read`.

choices.text: `r.Close()`
choices.why: Refused: `r.Close undefined (type io.Reader has no field or method Close)`.

choices.text: `r.(io.Closer).Close()`
choices.why: It compiles, and panics for every reader that has no `Close`, such as a `*strings.Reader`.

choices.text: `if c, ok := r.(io.Closer); ok { c.Close() }`
choices.why: Right. It asks for the capability and only uses it when the answer is yes.

choices.text: `if r != nil { r.(*os.File).Close() }`
choices.why: Files are not the only readers with `Close`, and any other non-nil reader panics here.

prompt: `r` is an `io.Reader`. Why is `r.(bytes.Buffer)` refused when `r.(*bytes.Buffer)` compiles?
hint: Lesson 26: which method set has `Read`?

choices.text: Type assertions only accept pointer types
choices.why: `.(float64)` and `.(string)` are assertions to non-pointer types and compiled throughout this lesson.

choices.text: The method `Read` belongs to the pointer's method set alone
choices.why: Right, so a value without the `*` never satisfies the interface, and an assertion bound to fail is refused as impossible.

choices.text: The buffer was stored with `&`, so the assertion has to repeat the `&`
choices.why: What was stored is only known at run time; a mismatch there would panic, not be refused.

choices.text: Structs like `bytes.Buffer` are refused in assertions
choices.why: Lesson 28's `r.(*Player)` asserted to a pointer to a struct, and a struct type works where the method set fits.

prompt: In `switch v := x.(type)`, with `x` an `any`, what is the type of `v` inside `case string:`?
hint: This case names exactly one type.

choices.text: `any`, the type of `x`
choices.why: That is a case listing several types. A case naming one type gives `v` that type.

choices.text: `string`, the type that case names
choices.why: Right, which is why `%q` and `len(v)` work in that case with no assertion written.

choices.text: `*string`, a pointer to the value inside
choices.why: `v` is the value itself, of the case's type; no pointer is involved.

choices.text: Whatever type `x` held when the program was compiled
choices.why: `x` holds nothing at compile time; the case is chosen while the program runs.

prompt: In `case int, float64:` of the same switch, what is `v`?
hint: The compiler said it in `mismatched types ... and untyped int`.

choices.text: An `any`, the type of `x`, since `v` cannot be both
choices.why: Right. `v` cannot be two types at once, so it keeps the interface type, and `v * 2` was refused.

choices.text: A `float64`, the wider of the two
choices.why: Go converts nothing implicitly, lesson 10; an `int` stays an `int`.

choices.text: An `int`, the first type listed
choices.why: Then `2.5` could not be in it. The order of the list does not choose a type.

choices.text: Whichever matched, so `v * 2` compiles
choices.why: `%T` prints whichever matched, but the compiler refused `v * 2` in that case.

prompt: `kind` has `case nil`, `case int, float64`, `case string` and `default`. Which case does a nil `*int` reach?
hint: What does the interface holding it contain?

choices.text: `case nil`, since the pointer is nil
choices.why: `case nil` matches an interface with no type, and this one holds the type `*int`.

choices.text: `case int, float64`, since it points at an `int`
choices.why: `*int` and `int` are different types, and a case matches the type exactly.

choices.text: `default`
choices.why: Right: the run printed `something else: *int`.

choices.text: None: the switch panics on a nil pointer
choices.why: A type switch reads the type word only, and never follows the pointer.

prompt: In a type switch the compiler refuses the statement ___, because the next case would receive a `v` of a different type.
hint: Lesson 19 used it to run the body of the next case.

prompt: Your error type `*NotFound` has an `Error` method, and you add a `String` method that returns something else. What does `fmt.Println(err)` print?
hint: Which case comes first in `fmt`'s switch?

choices.text: What `String` returns, as the newest method
choices.why: The order methods were written in means nothing; the order of the cases in `fmt` decides.

choices.text: What `Error` returns, since `case error` comes first
choices.why: Right. `Both` printed `from Error`, for the same reason.

choices.text: Both strings, one after the other
choices.why: A switch runs one case and stops; it never runs two.

choices.text: Nothing: two describing methods make the call ambiguous and it panics
choices.why: There is no ambiguity in a switch: the first case that matches runs.

prompt: Put in order what happens to the line `through a bufio.Writer` in the second version of `report`.
hint: It ends on the terminal.
items: `w.(FlushWriter)` asks whether the writer also has `Flush`

prompt: Which of these are true? Choose all that apply.
hint: One for each section, and two traps.

choices.text: An interface built by embedding is satisfied implicitly, like every other interface
choices.why: Yes. `*bufio.Writer` fits `FlushWriter` without naming it.

choices.text: The form `v, ok := x.(T)` does not panic, whatever `x` holds
choices.why: Yes, even for an empty interface, as `email` showed.

choices.text: `x.(T)` compiles with `x` an `int` variable
choices.why: Refused: `n (variable of type int) is not an interface`.

choices.text: `case nil` matches a nil pointer stored in an interface
choices.why: Only an interface with no type; the nil `*int` went to `default`.

choices.text: A type switch can name interfaces in its cases, and their order matters
choices.why: Yes. `fmt` checks `error` before `Stringer`, and that order picks the method.
